    Industry News: This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.
    • Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

    Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

    A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

    Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

    Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, stated:.

    “A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”.

    The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

    One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

    The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

    Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

    After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

    These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

    The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

    Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

    The memory findings were more complicated.

    Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

    By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

    One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

    Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in latest information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

    However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

    Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

    Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

    Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

    These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

    The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

    Blood samples also revealed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

    Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

    The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    • Recent findings suggest that what's your FI number?
    • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
    • The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

    The one number that changes everything.

    Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

    The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

    Recent findings suggest that here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

    The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

    In a recent development, the annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

    Industry observers note that this limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:.

    The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:.

    In a recent development, the annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

    This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

    When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — at the moment $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

    Industry observers note that let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

    According to recent reports, at the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

    Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

    Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:.

    The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

    If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

    Sources indicate that one of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

    It has been revealed that for 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

    This strategy is powerful because:.

    The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

    The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

    Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

    Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

    Sources indicate that the current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

    A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

    Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

    Industry observers note that pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

    Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

    Industry observers note that pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

    In a recent development, front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

    Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

    If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

    According to recent reports, pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

    In a recent development, if your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

    Pro tip: With the exemption sunset approaching in 2026, large transfers should be planned now rather than later.

    It has been revealed that in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 per recipient without any tax consequences or reporting requirements. Above that amount, you file Form 709 but still won't owe tax until you've exceeded your $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Married couples can give up to $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

    No. The recipient of a gift never pays income tax or gift tax on the gift. The giver is responsible for any gift tax reporting (Form 709) and any tax that might be owed. Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

    In a recent development, you must file Form 709 with your tax return for that year. The amount above $18,000 reduces your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption ($13.61 million). You won't owe any actual gift tax unless your cumulative lifetime gifts exceed the lifetime exemption. Think of it as paperwork, not a penalty.

    According to recent reports, yes, though the amount matters. You can give $18,000 per year with no reporting. You and your spouse together can give $36,000. For larger down payment gifts, you'll file Form 709 and use some of your $13.61 million lifetime exemption — but no tax is owed. Your mortgage lender will require a gift letter confirming the money is a gift, not a loan.

    It has been revealed that no. The unlimited marital deduction means you can transfer any amount to your US citizen spouse completely free of gift tax and estate tax. No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

    Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

    The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

    #69443. Industry News: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1394 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
    • A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
    • Recent findings suggest that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

    A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

    Recent findings suggest that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

    According to recent reports, better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It notes nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

    According to recent reports, we wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

    Recent findings suggest that the short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

    For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

    In a recent development, here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

    This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

    These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

    To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

    We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

    Two design choices shaped the work:.

    We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

    In a recent development, distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

    All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

    In a recent development, no single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

    A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That claims nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It highlights how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

    Industry observers note that linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

    Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

    CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

    Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

    Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

    In a recent development, one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

    According to recent reports, looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

    Industry observers note that up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

    Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

    Recent findings suggest that more data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

    In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

    It has been revealed that what does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

    Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

    The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

    Dharma-AI R&D · We Make AI Your Model.

    #69440. Breaking: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (848 w)

    Breaking: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
    • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
    • It has been revealed that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

    The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

    The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

    It has been revealed that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

    After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

    The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

    Sources indicate that daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

    According to recent reports, scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

    Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

    We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

    We selected tasks using three criteria:.

    Recent findings suggest that radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

    According to recent reports, 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

    Recent findings suggest that 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

    Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

    It has been revealed that every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

    Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

    Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

    The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

    According to recent reports, cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

    Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

    Sources indicate that we’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

    According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.
